title: the words on the doorpost
hook: the little case on the doorframe; what's actually inside it
tomorrow: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset

segments.voice: That little case on the doorframe. Right side as you walk in, about shoulder height, often tilted. Some people touch it on the way out and kiss their fingertips, as quick as checking for keys. Most people assume the case is the thing. It isn't. The case is just a case. First, a guess: what's inside?
screen: `THE CASE ON THE DOORFRAME.` → `TOUCHED ON THE WAY OUT.` → `WHAT'S INSIDE?`

segments.voice: Inside is a tiny scroll, written by hand on parchment by a trained scribe with a quill. It carries a passage from the Torah that opens with six famous words, the Shema: hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one. The same passage says to write these words on the doorposts of your house. So people did, literally. Mezuzah is simply Hebrew for doorpost: the word for the frame became the word for the scroll. On the back, many scribes write one of God's names, Shaddai, which some read as the initials of guardian of the doors of Israel. Now the tilt. A famous medieval teacher, Rashi, said hang it upright. His grandson said lay it flat. Many Ashkenazi Jews, whose families come from central and eastern Europe, hang it at a slant: a little of both. Many Sephardi Jews hang it upright. And the touch? Not a lucky charm; the great teacher Maimonides warned against treating it as one. It's a reminder. Every time you cross the threshold, going out or coming home, you pass the words. And one more thing about this door: it doesn't check your beliefs or your family tree on the way in. However you got here, you're welcome to walk through.
screen: `A SCROLL, WRITTEN BY HAND.` · `HEAR, O ISRAEL.` · `UPRIGHT OR FLAT? A SLANT.` · `A REMINDER, NOT A CHARM.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Rest your fingertips on the nearest doorframe, or just picture your own front door. Breathe in. As you breathe out, think of one thing you'd like to carry through that door today. Then lift your hand.
The mezuzah. Doorpost, and the handwritten words fixed to it: hear, O Israel. First word on your strand.
screen: `THE MEZUZAH — your 1st word` → clicks onto an empty word-strand.

segments.voice: Your line: take the words with you. That's what the touch on the way out means. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO FLAMES, EIGHTEEN MINUTES BEFORE SUNSET.`

original.note: Hebrew: doorpost. the word for the frame became the word for the scroll on it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Jewish decoration on the door.
what it means: the words of the Shema, written by hand and fixed to the doorpost, touched on the way in and out.
what a scholar hears: Deuteronomy 6:9 and 11:20 command it; the slant settles Rashi against his grandson Rabbeinu Tam; Maimonides (Laws of Mezuzah 5:4) rejects using it as an amulet.

story.title: the prisoner at the door
story.text: Soldiers are sent to arrest a Roman nobleman, the emperor's own relative, because he has become a Jew. Twice he talks his captors into joining him, so the emperor sends a third squad with strict orders: don't talk to him. As they lead him out of his house, he puts his hand on the mezuzah. They can't help asking what it is. A human king sits inside while his guards stand outside, he says; here, the people sit inside, and God keeps watch from outside.
story.source: Babylonian Talmud, Avodah Zarah 11a (the story of Onkelos)

wrong.truth: it's a reminder: handwritten words from the Torah, the Shema, fixed where you'll pass them every day.
